# Scatter plots {#sec-scatter-plot}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")
# use font
showtext::showtext_auto()
# set theme
ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_doom(
    base_size = 14))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_doom()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_doom()`, built from Doom (1993): a scorched brown background, a hellfire red frame and title, red, orange, gunmetal, armor green, blue key, and yellow key marks, and an Impact title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1993)
doom_pcs <- tibble(
  pc_id = 1:200,
  cpu_mhz = round(runif(200, min = 25, max = 100)),
  fps = round(pmin(35, 0.45 * cpu_mhz +
                     rnorm(200, mean = 0, sd = 3)), 1))
labs_scatter <- labs(
  title = "Doom frame rates",
  subtitle = "Frames per second by processor speed",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  x = "CPU speed (MHz)", y = "Frames per second")
ggp2_scatter <- doom_pcs |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = cpu_mhz,
      y = fps)) +
  geom_point()

ggp2_scatter +
  labs_scatter
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ two numeric (continuous) variables**
:::

::::

## Description

Scatter plots are used to display two continuous variables.

If one of the continuous variables is assumed to affect the other (i.e., `outcome` vs. `predictor`), place the `outcome` on the `y` axis and the `predictor` on the `x` axis.

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Install packages.
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_scatter
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::


::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

When *Doom* came out in December 1993, the first question every PC owner asked was how well it would run on their machine. A faster processor drew more frames per second, but only up to a point: the Doom engine never drew more than 35 frames per second, no matter how fast the computer was. We'll simulate 200 PCs with processors between 25 and 100 MHz (`cpu_mhz`, drawn with `runif()`). Each PC's frame rate (`fps`) is 0.45 frames per megahertz, plus some noise from `rnorm()` (for the graphics card, the RAM, and whatever else was running), and `pmin()` caps it at 35. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 200 PCs every time you run the code below.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_scatter
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1993) # same 200 PCs every time the code runs
doom_pcs <- tibble(
  pc_id = 1:200, # 200 different PCs, one row each
  cpu_mhz = round(runif(200, min = 25, max = 100)), # processor speeds spread evenly from 25 to 100 MHz
  fps = round(
    pmin(35, 0.45 * cpu_mhz + # faster processors, more frames (Doom caps out at 35)
           rnorm(200, mean = 0, sd = 3)), # random PC to PC noise
    1 # one decimal place
    )
  )
glimpse(doom_pcs)
```
:::

## Distribution

A scatter plot shows how one variable changes as the other changes. In the Doom data, the frame rate climbs in a straight line with the processor speed, wobbles around that line, and then hits a ceiling. Below we'll move from the PCs, to a picture, to the formula.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first six PCs.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_scatter
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(doom_pcs)
```
:::

Faster processors tend to have higher frame rates. Below we fit a straight line to the PCs at or below 66 MHz (well under the cap) with `lm()`, and count how many PCs landed exactly on the 35 frame ceiling.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_scatter
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
slow_pcs <- doom_pcs |>
  filter(cpu_mhz <= 66)
slow_fit <- lm(fps ~ cpu_mhz, data = slow_pcs)
coef(slow_fit)
sigma(slow_fit)
sum(doom_pcs$fps == 35)
```
:::

The fitted slope is about `r round(coef(slow_fit)[["cpu_mhz"]], 2)` frames per megahertz (close to the 0.45 we built in), and the typical distance from the line (`sigma()`) is about `r round(sigma(slow_fit), 1)` frames. `r sum(doom_pcs$fps == 35)` of the 200 PCs are stuck at exactly 35 frames per second.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

The graph below adds the line we built the data from (`geom_abline()`), a ribbon two standard deviations above and below it, and a dashed line at the 35 frame cap. Most of the points fall inside the ribbon until the line runs into the cap, and from there the points pile up in a flat row.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_scatter
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
ggplot(doom_pcs, aes(x = cpu_mhz, y = fps)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0.45 * cpu_mhz - 6, ymax = 0.45 * cpu_mhz + 6),
              fill = "#8A8D8F", alpha = 1 / 4) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 0.45, color = "#F2C14E",
              linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 35, linetype = "dashed", color = "#D63A1E") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "CPU speed (MHz)", y = "Frames per second")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

Each PC's frame rate is a draw from a [normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution) centered on a straight line (the [simple linear regression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_linear_regression) model), and then capped:

$$
\text{fps}_i = \min\left(35, \; 0.45 \times \text{MHz}_i + \varepsilon_i\right), \quad \varepsilon_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, \; 3)
$$

About 95% of the points land within $2 \times 3 = 6$ frames of the line, which is the ribbon in **DRAW IT**. The line reaches the cap at $35 / 0.45 \approx `r round(35 / 0.45)`$ MHz, so above that speed most of the PCs sit on the ceiling. A cap like this is called [censoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censoring_(statistics)), and it bends the relationship: the correlation for all 200 PCs is `r round(cor(doom_pcs$cpu_mhz, doom_pcs$fps), 2)`, but a straight line fit to all of them would underestimate the slope for the slow PCs and overestimate it for the fast ones. Try removing `pmin(35, ...)` and the points keep climbing in a straight line.

## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::



  - Create labels with `labs()`

  - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

  - Map `cpu_mhz` to the `x` axis

  - Map `fps` to the `y` axis

  - Add `geom_point()`

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_scatter
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
labs_scatter <- labs(
  title = "Doom frame rates",
  subtitle = "Frames per second by processor speed",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  x = "CPU speed (MHz)", y = "Frames per second")
ggp2_scatter <- doom_pcs |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = cpu_mhz,
      y = fps)) +
  geom_point()

ggp2_scatter +
  labs_scatter
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::


If multiple points occupy the same value position, use transparency (`alpha`) to improve visibility.

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_scatter
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_scatter <- labs(
  title = "Doom frame rates",
  subtitle = "Frames per second by processor speed",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  x = "CPU speed (MHz)", y = "Frames per second")
ggp2_scatter <- doom_pcs |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = cpu_mhz,
      y = fps)) +
  geom_point()

ggp2_scatter +
  labs_scatter
```
